narrative:
The law school’s decision rests on a model that predicts whether a student will pass the bar exam on the first attempt. For you, this model calculated an 82.9 percent probability of failing the bar exam. In other words, based on the patterns in the data, your academic profile suggests a very high risk of not passing, which is why your application was denied.

The strongest reason for this outcome was your class standing in the third year. You were in the first decile, meaning you ranked in the bottom ten percent of your class. By contrast, accepted students typically sit around the sixth decile. This was the single biggest factor pushing the prediction toward bar exam failure. The next most important factor was your first-year class standing, where you were in the second decile, still far below the average of the sixth decile for accepted students. This also pushed strongly toward failure, though not as strongly as your third-year record.

The third most influential factor was your undergraduate GPA. Here, the effect was slightly in your favor: despite your 2.60 GPA being lower than the accepted average of 3.23, the model treated it as a small point toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive nudge was far too weak to outweigh the two class-ranking indicators.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic standing in your current or future coursework, especially in your later years, and consider retaking the LSAT to strengthen your overall application.
